Chapter 7: The Struggle to Belong — Life as a Defector
Freedom—it isn’t really a finish line, is it? Turns out, it’s more like a journey. For someone who’s managed to escape, that very first taste of liberty can be surprisingly bittersweet. Suddenly, the world stretches out, wide and overwhelming, full of choices they’d never even dreamed of having. And with all those choices, uncertainty rushes in—and with uncertainty, well, comes a whole new kind of fear.
Picture our poet, arriving in a new land and finding himself surrounded by others who’ve made that same risky journey. Some folks throw themselves into their new lives, eager to work, to study, to start over. But not everyone can move on so easily. For many, memories from the past linger, making it tough to let go of the world they left behind. Even among fellow defectors, there’s still this deep sense of isolation—as though everyone speaks the same language of loss, just in different dialects.
Every single day brings a new challenge. Suddenly, the rules have changed. Expectations aren’t what they used to be. Even basic things—like buying groceries, making a friend, or just finding a place to call home—start to feel like tests. The poet wrestles with the language, the customs, and that constant feeling of being on the outside looking in.
But it’s not all struggle. There are moments of unexpected kindness, too. Maybe it’s a teacher who patiently goes over a lesson one more time. Or a neighbor who drops by with a warm meal. Even just a stranger’s easy smile—a smile without suspicion—can feel like a lifeline. These small gestures remind the poet that yes, it’s possible to build new connections, to carve out a place in this unfamiliar world.
Yet, the past never really disappears. News from home trickles in, and it’s rarely good. The poet can’t help but worry about the family left behind, or friends who might’ve paid the price for his escape. Guilt and grief become steady companions, sticking around even in moments of happiness.
Most people in this new country don’t know much about where the defectors came from. Sometimes there’s curiosity, sometimes suspicion, sometimes pity. The poet learns to share his story carefully, always trying to protect himself from being misunderstood or judged. And over time, he realizes that the biggest hurdle isn’t just surviving—it’s finding that sense of belonging. It’s about learning how to be himself in a world that’s both brand new and, at times, indifferent.
The whole process is slow—filled with setbacks but also small victories. Each new day brings another lesson, another chance to grow. Little by little, the poet learns to trust again, to hope, to picture a future that isn’t just about fear.
It’s never easy. But you know what? It’s possible.
